summary: Otilonium bromide is a quaternary ammonium antispasmodic used to relieve abdominal pain, cramping, and spasm associated with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and other functional gastrointestinal disorders. It acts locally on intestinal smooth muscle - inhibiting L-type calcium channels and antagonizing muscarinic and tachykinin receptors - and is very poorly absorbed from the gut, giving it a gut-selective spasmolytic effect with minimal systemic anticholinergic exposure. The usual adult dose is 40 mg two to three times daily, taken before meals. It is NOT approved by the US FDA; it is used in Europe, Latin America, and Asia under products such as Spasmomen / Spasmoctyl. Dosing and recommendations are based on the European/manufacturer summary of product characteristics (SmPC) and clinical use rather than FDA labeling.

moa: Otilonium bromide is a locally acting intestinal spasmolytic. It inhibits the entry of calcium into gastrointestinal smooth-muscle cells by blocking L-type (and some T-type) voltage-dependent calcium channels, and it antagonizes muscarinic cholinergic receptors and tachykinin (neurokinin NK1/NK2) receptors involved in intestinal contraction and visceral hypersensitivity. The combined effect reduces smooth-muscle tone and spasm and relieves abdominal pain. Because the molecule is a quaternary ammonium compound that is poorly absorbed and concentrates in the gut wall, its action is largely confined to the gastrointestinal tract with little systemic anticholinergic effect.

monitor: Symptomatic response; investigate persistent or alarm symptoms (weight loss, bleeding, anemia)

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy. Although systemic absorption is low, the manufacturer advises that it should be used during pregnancy only if clearly necessary and after weighing potential benefit against risk. (Based on European SmPC; the drug is not FDA-approved.)
lact: There are limited data on excretion into breast milk. Given the minimal systemic absorption, exposure to the infant is expected to be low, but caution is advised and use during breastfeeding should be only when considered necessary. (Based on European SmPC.)
renal: No specific dose adjustment has been established for renal impairment; systemic absorption is minimal and most of the drug is eliminated unchanged in feces/bile.
hepatic: No specific dose adjustment has been established for hepatic impairment. Elimination is predominantly biliary/fecal of the poorly absorbed drug.

major: No clinically significant major drug interactions established (low systemic absorption)
moderate: Additive effects possible with other anticholinergic agents (theoretical)
interactions.food: Taken before meals; no specific food restriction beyond timing.

rare: Anticholinergic-type effects (dry mouth, blurred vision) - rare given poor absorption

pearls: NOT FDA-approved - marketed in Europe, Latin America and Asia (e.g., Spasmomen); recommendations follow the European SmPC / clinical use, not FDA labeling
Gut-selective: poorly absorbed quaternary ammonium, so it relieves intestinal spasm with little systemic anticholinergic effect
Multimodal action - L-type calcium-channel block plus muscarinic and tachykinin (NK) receptor antagonism - underlies its effect on IBS pain and visceral hypersensitivity
Use as symptomatic therapy alongside dietary/lifestyle measures; always exclude organic disease in patients with alarm features
Taken before meals to pre-empt postprandial spasm
missed: If a dose is missed, take it before the next meal as soon as remembered. If it is almost time for the next scheduled dose, skip the missed one and continue the normal before-meal schedule. Do not take two doses together.
overdose: Experience with overdose is limited; because systemic absorption is very low, serious systemic toxicity is unlikely. In the event of a large ingestion, anticholinergic-type effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia, urinary retention) are theoretically possible. Management is supportive and symptomatic.
